lessons.title: Big O Notation
lessons.concept: Big O describes the upper bound of running time (worst case) as input size grows. Common: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).
lessons.worked_example: Single loop over n → O(n). Nested loop → O(n²). Binary search → O(log n).
mistakes: Confusing Big O with exact time

lessons.title: Complexity Reference
lessons.concept: Array: access O(1), search O(n). BST: search O(log n) avg. Hash: O(1) avg. Merge sort O(n log n). Quick sort worst O(n²).
lessons.worked_example: Hash table avg O(1), worst O(n). Binary search requires sorted array.
mistakes: Assuming BST always O(log n) (degenerate → O(n))
Assuming quick sort always O(n log n)

practice.question: What does Big O describe?
practice.explanation: Big O = upper bound of running time (worst case).

practice.question: Hash table average time complexity?
practice.explanation: Hash table average O(1); worst O(n) with collisions.

practice.question: Big-O notation describes:

options.B: Asymptotic upper bound on growth as input size increases

practice.explanation: Big-O bounds how resource usage grows for large inputs, ignoring constants and lower-order terms - not wall-clock seconds.

practice.question: Dropping constants, 3n + 20 is:
practice.explanation: Big-O keeps only the dominant growth term: 3n + 20 -> O(n) (the constant 3 and additive 20 are asymptotically irrelevant).

practice.question: What is the space complexity of an iterative binary search?

options.B: O(1) - only a few index variables

practice.explanation: The iterative version keeps only lo, hi and mid: constant extra space. (Recursion adds O(log n) call-stack frames.)

practice.question: Amortised O(1) append on a dynamic array means:

options.A: Every append is exactly one instruction
options.B: Occasional O(n) resizes average out to constant time per append

practice.explanation: Doubling capacity makes the total copy cost over n appends linear, so average cost per append is O(1) even though a single append occasionally costs O(n).

practice.question: Two sequential loops of n iterations each give complexity:
practice.explanation: Sequential loops add: n + n = 2n, which is O(n). Only nested loops multiply into O(n^2).

questions.question: Merge sort worst-case?
questions.explanation: Merge sort always O(n log n), stable, needs extra space.

questions.question: Quick sort worst case?
questions.explanation: Quick sort worst O(n²) (e.g., sorted input with bad pivot).

questions.question: Binary search requirement?
questions.explanation: Binary search requires a sorted array.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search?
questions.explanation: Each step halves the range: after k steps the range is n/2^k = 1, so k = log2 n -> O(log n).

questions.question: Sorting n elements with comparison-based algorithms has a best-known worst case of:
questions.explanation: The comparison-model lower bound is Omega(n log n); merge sort and heap sort achieve O(n log n) worst case (quick sort: average case).
questions.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Nested loops of n iterations each over the same input imply complexity:
questions.explanation: Two nested n-iteration loops perform about n*n = n^2 body executions: O(n^2). Sequential loops add (O(2n) = O(n)); only nesting multiplies.

questions.question: Which pair is correctly ordered from slowest to fastest growth?

options.A: O(n^2), O(n log n), O(n), O(log n), O(1)
options.B: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2)
options.C: O(1), O(n), O(log n), O(n^2), O(n log n)
options.D: O(log n), O(1), O(n), O(n^2), O(n log n)

questions.explanation: Slowest to fastest growth: polynomial first - O(n^2) > O(n log n) > O(n) > O(log n) > O(1). Option A lists exactly this decreasing order (slowest first).

questions.question: What is the space complexity of merge sort (excluding the output array)?
questions.explanation: Merge sort recurses log n levels deep, using O(log n) stack space; the temporary merge buffers (if allocated per call) can add O(n).
questions.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Which growth rate is O(n log n)?
questions.explanation: Efficient comparison sorts (merge/heap sort) are O(n log n). Binary search is O(log n); hash lookup average O(1); array access O(1).

questions.explanation: The master theorem case 2 (a=2, b=2, f(n)=n): T(n) = Theta(n log n).
